q: A student heats a sealed flask of liquid water until it is all steam. Which statement best describes the molecules in the steam?
opts: They are still H₂O molecules, but now far apart.
Each H₂O molecule has split into hydrogen and oxygen atoms.
The water has become a different compound as it boiled.
The molecules shrink, so the gas takes up less space.
exp: Boiling is a physical change. The H₂O molecules stay intact; only their motion and spacing change.
why: Boiling is a physical change, so the molecules are not split apart. Splitting water needs electrolysis.
The substance is still water. A different compound would need a chemical change.
The molecules do not change size; the spaces between them grow, so the gas spreads out.

q: You crush a block of rock salt into powder and then dissolve the powder in water. How should the two changes be classified?
opts: Crushing is physical and dissolving is chemical.
Both crushing and dissolving are physical changes.
Crushing is chemical and dissolving is physical.
Both crushing and dissolving are chemical changes.
exp: The salt keeps its composition in both steps, so both are physical changes.
why: Dissolving only spreads the salt through the water. No new substance forms, so it is physical.
Crushing only changes the size of the pieces. The composition stays the same, so it is physical.
Neither process makes a new substance. Both are physical.

q: A student drops an antacid tablet into vinegar and sees bubbles. What does this show?
opts: Only a physical change, because the tablet gets smaller.
A change of state of the tablet into a gas.
A chemical change, because a new gas formed.
A mixture forming, because two substances were combined.
exp: Gas formation is an indicator of a chemical change.
why: A shrinking tablet alone could be dissolving, but bubbles of gas signal a new substance forming.
The tablet does not turn into gas; a gas forms from the reaction between the tablet and the vinegar.
Combining substances can make a mixture, but bubbles of new gas show a reaction took place.

q: Steel wool is massed, burned and massed again. The mass went up by 0.38 g. What is the best explanation?
opts: Burning always adds mass to metals.
The iron atoms got heavier from the heat.
The steel wool absorbed water from the air.
Oxygen from the air combined with the iron.
exp: Iron plus oxygen forms iron(III) oxide, which has more mass than the iron alone.
why: Burning does not simply add mass. The extra mass comes from a specific reactant.
Heat does not make atoms heavier. The mass gain comes from additional atoms joining the iron.
Nothing in the data points to water. Burning iron combines with oxygen.

q: Two samples of pure copper are compared: a tiny wire and a large block. Which property is identical?
opts: Density
Volume
Length
Mass
exp: Density is intensive, so it does not depend on how much copper there is.
why: The block takes up more space, so volume differs. Volume is extensive.
Length depends on the size of the sample, so it is extensive.
The block has more matter, so its mass is greater. Mass is extensive.

q: A jar holds pieces of Cu and Zn mixed together, written Cu & Zn. How should it be labeled?
opts: An element, since both Cu and Zn are elements.
A mixture, because the & shows two substances.
A compound, since two types of atom are present.
A solution that cannot be separated.
exp: The & symbol marks a mixture of two elements.
why: Each of the two is an element, but the jar holds two different substances together, which is not one element.
Compounds are written as one bonded formula. The & shows separate substances.
Mixtures can be separated by physical methods, so the claim is false.

q: A particle drawing shows several separate, identical Br₂ molecules. How should the sample be labeled?
opts: A compound, because it contains molecules of bonded atoms.
A mixture, because there are so many particles present.
An element, because only bromine atoms are present.
A compound, because the atoms in each molecule are bonded.
exp: Identical Br₂ molecules contain one type of atom, so the sample is an element.
why: Molecules can contain only one type of atom. Br₂ has only bromine atoms.
Many identical particles still make a pure substance; a mixture needs different particles.
Bonding alone does not make a compound. A compound needs two or more types of atoms.

q: Muddy water is poured through filter paper. What passes through and what stays on the paper?
opts: Dissolved salt stays; undissolved dirt passes through.
Everything passes through because it is wet.
Water decomposes and the hydrogen stays on the paper.
Clear liquid passes through; undissolved dirt stays.
exp: Filtration separates undissolved solids from liquids.
why: This reverses the process. Dissolved particles pass through filter paper.
The paper traps solid particles that are too large to pass through.
Filtering is a physical method and does not break water apart.

q: How would you recover pure water from salt water?
opts: Boil it and condense the steam.
Run an electric current through the mixture.
Add more salt until the water separates.
Filter the salt water through paper.
exp: Distillation uses the difference in boiling points; the salt stays behind.
why: An electric current would decompose water into gases; it would not separate it from the salt.
Adding salt just makes the solution more concentrated.
Dissolved salt passes through filter paper, so the water would not be pure.

q: Which approach would you use to break water into hydrogen and oxygen?
opts: Distillation, a physical method.
Electrolysis, a chemical method.
Filtration, a physical method.
Evaporation, a physical method.
exp: Water is a compound, so separating its elements takes a chemical method.
why: Distillation only boils and condenses, so the water stays water.
Filtration separates solids from liquids and cannot split a compound.
Evaporation turns water into vapor but does not break the molecules apart.

q: A student writes NaCl & H₂O for a drawing. What does the drawing most likely show?
opts: A heterogeneous mixture of sand and water.
A compound containing sodium and chlorine.
Salt water, a homogeneous mixture.
A pure substance made of three elements.
exp: The & shows two substances mixed together; salt in water is the same throughout.
why: The formulas show salt and water, and dissolved salt is uniform throughout.
NaCl alone would be the compound; the & and H₂O show a second substance.
A pure substance has no & in its code; this is two substances together.

q: A tea light is melted, and then a different one is lit. Which statement is correct?
opts: Melting is chemical; burning is physical.
Both are chemical changes.
Both are physical changes.
Melting is physical; burning is chemical.
exp: Melted wax is still wax, but burning makes new substances.
why: This swaps them. Melted wax is still wax.
Melting does not form a new substance.
Burning wax reacts with oxygen and forms new substances.

q: A student says "Br₂ is a molecule, so it must be a compound." What is the best reply?
opts: Wrong, because Br₂ has only one type of atom.
Correct, because it has a subscript of two.
Wrong, because Br₂ is actually a mixture of two things.
Correct, since all molecules are compounds.
exp: A compound needs two or more different atom types. Br₂ is an element made of molecules.
why: A subscript only counts atoms. It does not decide whether something is a compound.
There is no & in Br₂, so it is a single pure substance.
Not all molecules are compounds. Molecules of a single element exist.

q: Which substance is a heterogeneous mixture?
opts: Brass
Soil
Air
Gasoline
why: Brass is the same throughout, so it is homogeneous.
Air is the same throughout, so it is homogeneous.
Gasoline looks uniform, so it is homogeneous.

q: A post-1982 penny is cut and left overnight in hydrochloric acid. It loses 0.19 g and bubbles formed. What is the best conclusion?
opts: The copper coating melted in the acid, a physical change.
The acid just washed dirt off the penny.
The zinc core reacted with the acid, a chemical change.
Water inside the penny evaporated during the night.
exp: Bubbles and mass loss show that the zinc reacted with the acid.
why: Melting would need heat, and bubbles would not form. Acid does not melt copper.
Dirt cannot account for bubbles and a lost mass of 0.19 g.
A penny has no water to evaporate, and evaporation would not form bubbles.

q: You stir sand into salt water, filter it, then boil the filtrate. Which is the correct order of methods?
opts: Distillation first, then filtration.
Filtration first, then chromatography.
Chromatography first, then evaporation.
Filtration first, then distillation.
exp: Remove the sand first, then boil off the water from the salt solution.
why: Boiling first leaves sand and salt together, so the order does not separate them.
Chromatography separates substances by adherence to a surface and is not how you recover water from salt water.
Chromatography does not remove sand from water.

q: A flashlight beam is visible as it passes through a glass of fog-like cloudy liquid. Which conclusion is best supported?
opts: The liquid is a colloid, because it scatters the light.
The liquid is a true solution, because the beam passed through.
The liquid is a pure element, because it is cloudy and uniform.
The liquid is a suspension, because the beam is visible in it.
exp: Particles of about 1 nm to 1000 nm scatter light (the Tyndall effect) and stay mixed, so the liquid is a colloid.
why: A true solution would not scatter the beam, so the beam would not be visible.
Being cloudy says nothing about being an element; it is a mixture.
A suspension would also settle on standing, which this liquid does not do.

q: A baker makes a mousse by whipping air into a thick liquid, and a jelly by setting a liquid inside a solid network. Which pair of names fits?
opts: The mousse is an emulsion and the jelly is a foam.
The mousse is a foam and the jelly is a gel.
The mousse is a sol and the jelly is an aerosol.
The mousse is a gel and the jelly is a solid sol.
exp: A gas dispersed in a liquid is a foam. A liquid dispersed in a solid is a gel.
why: An emulsion is a liquid in a liquid, and a foam is a gas in a liquid, so these are swapped.
A sol is a solid in a liquid, and an aerosol has a gas as its medium.
A gel is a liquid in a solid, so it describes the jelly, not the mousse.
